content:
Some thoughts and open questions about TFT’s design, grouped by topic. Most of these come from playing in Grandmaster - Low Challenger, so they lean toward that end of the game. The ideas are all mine; I used Claude to help organize and communicate them clearly.
Below is a quick prototype of one idea, followed by my working notes on TFT’s design. The notes are exploratory and not meant to be solid solutions; the prototype is what it looks like when I take one of them further.
Prototype: pool size indicator # A quick Unity mockup of one idea from these notes: showing how many copies of a champion are still available. Selecting a champion shows its remaining copies out of the total pool size, and the number updates live as units are rolled, bought, or adjusted. Hovering the number explains what it means for your shop.
Why show pool counts # Scouting the pool is a real skill in TFT, and showing pool counts would remove part of it. Scouting for items, positioning, and what people are building would still matter just as much, but counting copies would no longer separate experienced players from newer ones.
The bigger reason is newer players. As far as I know, the game never explains why you shouldn’t contest other players. Champion pools and pool sizes are core concepts that even lower-ranked players should understand, even if they don’t have a friend to explain it. Right now you learn it from a guide, a friend, or losing a lot.
The idea. A simple ratio on the champion’s info card (copies left in the pool out of the total pool size), which already holds a lot of information, plus a tooltip for newer players explaining that the ratio determines how likely they are to find that unit. Keep it general and readable rather than trying to show everything.
Should players have perfect knowledge of the pool? This is the real debate. One strong counterargument is that perfect information can be a problem in itself: if everyone knows exactly what’s left, everyone tends to make the same rational decisions, and lobbies get more uniform. Experienced players can already scout an approximate pool count, so the question is whether streamlining the new player experience is worth narrowing that gap. Put another way: is counting the pool a skill TFT should be testing?
My view is that while scouting is an important skill, it’s equally or more important for newer players to have something to point to when they can never seem to hit their units. Right now, many of them don’t even know the pool exists. Pool counts also better inform a player’s decision to pivot, which ties into the flexibility discussion below: if pivoting depends on reading the lobby correctly, pool counts make that read easier.
Details for a deeper dive. What exactly should count: copies in other players’ shops, in your own shop, on boards, on benches? These matter for implementation, but the general idea comes first.
Working notes # Everything below is my working notes: half-formed ideas, open questions, and things I’m still thinking through.
What do “flexible” and “creative” actually mean? # These words get thrown around all the time, but they’re really nebulous. Variety and monotony are much easier to define, so it might help to pin the fuzzier words to things that can actually be measured:
Flexibility: how predictable is a player’s final board from their early state? If you can call someone’s endgame comp from their opener or first augment, the game isn’t very flexible. Another angle: how do players who pivot place compared to players who stick to their line? Variety vs. monotony: how many distinct endgame boards show up in top 4, and how often does one player end up on the same endgame board across games? Creativity: maybe the feeling of making a choice the stats wouldn’t have recommended, and having it work. Hard to measure without just asking players. Line selection, theorycrafting, and endgame boards # At high levels, you usually pick a line and follow it. But I don’t think line selection itself is the problem. Your endgame board often gets locked in almost immediately, but the path there is probably the most creative and skill-expressive part of TFT: reading your opener, items, augments, and the lobby, and finding the right route through the midgame.
The problem is where those lines end up. Because stats are public, endgame boards are often the same handful of statistically strongest boards, so even after a creative midgame, the endgame can feel very monotonous. That’s why I think line selection/flexibility and theorycrafting are really closely related, maybe even the same problem: the path is creative, but the destination is mostly solved ahead of time.
Why flexibility matters # Flexibility is where a lot of skill expression comes from. If TFT were 100% rigid, players would just be waiting for the units they need to show up in their shop, which wouldn’t be very fun. The more flexible the game is, the more players can make use of any unit in their shop, and the more they can play around bad luck.
There’s a limit, though. If every unit were usable from every position, choosing units would feel meaningless, and the same problem would just show up with augments and items instead.
Committed vs. flexible players # From stage 2, almost every high-level player knows exactly what everyone else is going to play. Plans go wrong and people pivot in and out, but pivots are rare and generally avoided. There aren’t public stats on pivoting, but across thousands of games at Grandmaster and Challenger, that tells me most top players see it as negative EV. In the right spot, though, pivoting is the positive-EV play, and nothing tells you when you’re in that spot. Pivoting there means going against the general consensus and trusting your own intuition, which is exactly why a successful pivot feels so good. I think moments like that are some of the most engaging in TFT.
But that makes me think line selection isn’t actually that bad. If pivoting became positive EV in general, a few things would go wrong. Pivots would feel less engaging, since they’d be the expected play instead of a read that beats the odds. Everyone would be pivoting unpredictably, making it nearly impossible to play around other players’ actions, so the game would feel more like a volatile stock market: chaotic and high variance. And it would be overwhelming for newer players, who’d have more to consider at more stages of the game. Optimally, some players should have a clearly defined gameplan, and other players should be able to play flexibly around them. The question is how much.
Right now it feels like 7 to 8 players (basically everyone) have their gameplan decided from the start. Maybe it should be closer to 6 or 7. That raises a few questions:
Should flexible players be on even footing with committed ones? Better? Worse? If flexible play is better on average, everyone ends up in a game of chicken, waiting for someone else to lock in first, and at high levels flexibility would simply always be the right choice. I think flexibility should be, at its core, a comeback mechanic: a way to turn a spot that would normally be bad into a decent one, not something that beats a committed line on its own. What would move the ratio? The cost of changing direction (augment permanence, how permanent items are, how much value you lose selling), the reward for being uncontested (pool sizes, how much contesting hurts), and how much information players have (perfect scouting makes it easy to see who’s committed). When should players be forced into an endgame board? They obviously shouldn’t be switching boards every round. Pivoting should probably get more expensive as the game goes on, cheap early and costly late, with natural lock-in points around augments and the stage 4 rolldown. Since players are already committed in stage 2, pivoting is already negative-EV by stage 3, which suggests that curve might be too steep too early. Why lines lock in early # Part of what narrows the destinations is how changeable each piece of your board is:
Champions are the most flexible. You can always roll for more. Items are mostly set. You usually can’t change your components or finished items, though there are a few ways to do it a limited number of times per game. This has gotten much better over time. Augments are permanent. Once you have them, they’re there forever. Since augments are such a big part of your board’s strength and you can’t change them, your early augments narrow which endgame boards are realistically open to you, and switching later means ending up weaker than the player who stuck to their line. Suboptimal items do the same thing. If you find a good direction early, the game gets very simple.
One idea I’ve toyed with is making augments less set in stone, with some limited way to change them late in the game. To be clear, I don’t think it’s a good idea as it stands. It would be hard to implement, I haven’t thought it through, and it runs into a huge number of issues, for example:
Returning rewards only really works for combat augments. Augments that give gold or items can’t be taken back. On top of that, simply swapping these augments out is a terrible idea. It makes early combat augments feel horrendous, since players who take them go most of the game with fewer resources than everyone else. It might make endgame boards even more similar, since everyone could steer toward the strongest board more easily. Those are just the first few problems that come to mind. Unless every one of them got solved out very thoroughly, I think it would create more problems than it fixes.
Theorycrafting and public stats # Playing creatively in the endgame at a high level doesn’t really exist anymore. I think it used to, but now endgame boards are more of a stats-mashing contest over who can combine the things with the best numbers, since all the numbers are already out there. It makes the end of the game feel closer to a trivia game than a teambuilding game.
With this many players, no one can out-theorycraft the whole community. The meta gets posted online, and nearly everyone ends up with the same meta knowledge, apart from the very top, where Challenger players rely on their own intuition or study groups to min-max.
There are still rare chances to get ahead of the curve. At the start of Set 15, I noticed in the first patch that T-Hex was overtuned, before other players did and before it got buffed even more. But moments like that are uncommon. Trait Tracker and Trait Ladder augments might have created more of them, but now there are tools that solve the optimal boards for those too.
A big part of the payoff of creativity is the feeling of discovery, of being a pioneer. That’s hard to get when so many eyes are on the same game and the community solves things so quickly. I don’t think that’s easily solvable in the modern climate.
The other side of this is that players need something to ground them. Not every player wants to theorycraft at all, especially new players, and they shouldn’t have to. Being able to see the meta without playing 500 games is really healthy for the playerbase as a whole. The flip side is that if everything is already known, creative players don’t get rewarded for their creativity. That’s most true at the highest level of play, where things are the most optimized. At lower levels, you can probably get away with a lot more.
I’m not sure what the answer is. Stats sites work because the same choice is worth about the same in every game, so it averages out. Choices whose value depends more on the specific game (the lobby, what others are playing, what’s left in the pool) would be harder to solve ahead of time, but they’d also add variance, making the game more luck-based and harder to learn. That’s probably not worth the tradeoff.
Honestly, some centralization is probably unavoidable. The meta will always settle around a few comps. The obvious way around that is extremely high variance, but then the game becomes a gamblefest in its own right, and having to theorycraft every single game would be too mentally taxing for most players.
So I don’t think the goal is to make theorycrafting the norm. Ideally, it would be rewarding, or even optimal, in a small minority of games, maybe 1 in 10. Right now, I can’t think of a reason not to play a meta comp in almost any game.
Related: when I took a few months off TFT, it wasn’t because games lacked variety. There’s already a ton of variation between games. It was more that I’d learned so much that even with that much variety, games started to feel like going through the motions. Every game eventually gets to that point for a dedicated player, and honestly it’s a strength of TFT’s design that it took so long.
Scouting and matchmaking # Matchmaking is random for good reason. If you knew who you were fighting next, the game would turn into a twitch-reflex contest, which isn’t what TFT is trying to be.
I’d even question whether players should have perfect information on enemy boards and positioning. I don’t think the end-of-round positioning contest should really be part of the game. The catch is that players currently need to see enemy boards for other reasons: scouting champion counts, and clarity about what they’re fighting and losing against, which matters especially for newer players. But if that twitch-reflex repositioning went away, matchmaking could become more predictable and feel fairer.
I don’t mean literal round robin, just matchmaking that’s more uniform and predictable. It might still feel unfair sometimes, but it would at least feel fairer, especially in the late game, where fight order can be a huge swing in placements.
More uniform matchmaking would also avoid a lot of common frustrations, like lobbies where two players are on long streaks and some players keep running into them while others don’t, or endgames where it feels like you got screwed by fighting the same strong player several times in a row.
The two ideas really only work as a pair:
Predictable matchmaking on its own brings back the problem it’s trying to solve. If you know who you’re fighting next, last-second repositioning against that specific player becomes even stronger. Limited positioning information is what makes predictable matchmaking work. Knowing your opponent but not their final positioning turns it into a mind game instead of a reflex test. How much information players get matters a lot. If you can see an opponent’s comp and how they’ve positioned before, but not their final positioning this round, good players can still read and predict, so it stays a skill. If you can’t see anything, it’s basically a coin flip. Some partial information is probably the sweet spot. Guessing is at least a mental skill test rather than a twitch-reflex one, which feels more in the spirit of TFT.
Some things to work through:
Readability. Less visible information could make the game harder to follow for newer players, and for people watching streams or esports. Eliminations. Once players are knocked out, any fixed schedule has to adjust, with ghost fights or reshuffling. Feeling screwed after a loss # A lot of the time, losing can feel like you couldn’t have done anything. Statistically that’s obviously not true. There’s no perfect player, and probably no perfect game of TFT has ever been played. But it can be really unclear why certain decisions were bad. That’s why top players VOD review. Most players won’t, and how they feel one second after a game ends is pretty much how they’ll feel about that game overall.
The main things you can feel screwed by are items, rolldowns, matchmaking (see Scouting and matchmaking), and augments.
Items have improved a lot. You only really feel screwed by items maybe 1 in 50 games now, especially since many items can substitute for others, which keeps getting better with every update.
Rolldowns. The community’s understanding is that shops have some form of bad-luck protection, though how it works isn’t public. A past bug let players hit a 3-star Ryze in one shop, which people linked to it. In Set 15, a lot of players, including top players, reported terrible rolldown luck, and a popular theory was a bug in that system, but a dev said there was no such bug. Even I thought something was bugged at the time, just from the volume of reports. If there wasn’t a bug, was there something about that set that unintentionally made rolls feel worse?
Augments can’t be changed, so an early pick that doesn’t work out stays with you the whole game (see Line selection).
Other missing information # A lot of important information isn’t directly visible in the game, especially for newer players, though even experienced players would use some of it. Some examples:
Champions left in the pool (see the prototype at the top). Right now you have to scout other people’s boards and estimate. Cashouts for some traits and augments, which you can only find online. Damage taken from losing a round (the game may already show this somewhere; I don’t remember exactly). Probably many others I’m not thinking of. There’s also a lot of data that matters at high levels and basically just lives on websites: artifact stats, emblem stats, augment stats, comp stats, charm stats. Knowing or not knowing these can change a game a lot, and these days it feels less like intuition and more like having looked the numbers up ahead of time, which can feel bad.
I can see why some of this isn’t in the game, though. Some of it only really matters to a small number of high-level players, and for the playerbase as a whole it might not seem that important. Adding all of it would clutter the UI and make the game less inviting to newer players. An emblem’s average placement on a unit, for example, matters a lot at high levels, but it isn’t something you’d expect to see in game.
Stage by stage # Opener. Rule of thumb: match pairs and build the strongest board you can at any given time. Some players go for econ, but I find that pretty greedy and perform better just having a stronger board. I’d only make econ with no pairs and no strong early units worth keeping.
First augment. Depends on the meta, but usually econ or hero/lock-in augments. If you find a good direction early, the game gets very simple.
Stage 2. Strongest board, even if I’m not streaking. HP is very important, and I think streaking is a little overrated, though if you reach the end of the stage on a streak you obviously want to keep it. Levels usually within the range of 3/4/5. Level 6 on a hard-forced win streak is rare, and I think it’s usually a mistake.
Carousel. It has a nice comeback mechanic built in, since weaker players pick first. TFT has gotten a lot better about items in general: there’s still variance, but the item system is balanced well enough that most players can work around it in most games. I recall a dev specifically stating they wanted to remove it due to the twitch reflex nature of picking your item, and it has been removed a few times but always came back.
Neutral rounds. I recall a dev talking about wanting to remove neutral rounds and why they’re still here. If I remember right, one reason is that they give players a breather, which matters. But losing to them feels really bad while winning just feels normal, so the overall experience leans negative. Some questions:
Is there a reason players should be punished for a board that’s too weak here, or is it just filling the gap? What would TFT lose if it were just an empty round? Players would probably find the wait boring. What if it were a show match? Then players would feel like the outcome didn’t matter at all. A show match with real effects is a bigger problem, since stronger boards would get even more tempo and shift the meta a lot. Neutrals do make winning feel like it matters, even when it’s expected most of the time.
Stage 3. Level 5 on 1-cost reroll, 6 to 7 otherwise. Feels like cruise control: what you have at the start of the stage is likely what you’ll play the whole stage. That might be fine, since the later stages are intense. I usually use this time to scout and figure out my endgame plan.
Stage 4. Level 6 on 1 or 2-cost reroll, level 7 on 3-cost reroll, 8 otherwise. The meat and potatoes of the game and probably the stage people talk about most. Your board is expected to be locked in, big rolldowns happen, and you get your final augment. Most people would call this the climax of a TFT game. Does it have to be? I think it’s in a fine spot as is.
Stage 5 to endgame. If your board isn’t online here, you’re done. Some win-streaking fast 9 boards come online at this stage and will finish you off if you aren’t already out.
Other thoughts # Metas. This is probably what high-level players talk about most. A meta can get stale or unbalanced, but when people call a meta “bad,” they usually mean it isn’t very skill expressive: a few outliers should almost always be taken, not getting them means losing most of the time, and even better players have few ways around that luck.
Lower vs. higher tiers. There’s a big gap between the general playerbase and high-level players. Meta perception is really different, and simpler comps are seen as much stronger at lower tiers (I remember a friend complaining about Yordles when they were mediocre). Level distribution is different too, and a lot of lower-tier players like to force the same comp over and over. Honestly, they should be able to. It shouldn’t be viable at higher ranks, or the game becomes a slot machine. But at what rank should forcing stop being viable?
Retention. The meta and bug issues are mostly about retaining players rather than gaining new ones. Part of me wonders how important retention is, since a game can be really fun for a while and then fall off, and that’s fine. But as a company, it’s clearly important. I think Riot has caught onto this by making the early patches of a set higher variance and more fun, then more balanced and geared toward returning players later. Of course, that assumes they know how a patch will play out ahead of time, which they can’t fully.
New player experience. I suspect it’s what Riot worries about most. There’s a lot going on, more than a classic tutorial could teach intuitively, so it can be hard to get into, though TFT has gotten much better about this over time. It’s been a long time since I was a new player, and even my friends are mostly Platinum to Diamond now, so I don’t have much insight here.
Engine bugs. There are a lot right now, and they affect players at every level, but I assume they’re already known and being worked on.
Things I haven’t thought much about:
Positioning. It’s never been my strength, and it feels nebulous to me. Game length, which I think Riot has been trying to shorten recently. Combat readability. I’m not really a visuals person. Other game modes. I haven’t played them much, so I can’t say much. I do find Tocker’s Trials interesting, but it’s missing replayability for something so short, so it’s clearly in its early stages.
summary: A Unity prototype of a champion pool indicator, plus working notes on Teamfight Tactics’ design from a Grandmaster to Challenger player: flexibility, public stats, matchmaking, and more.
title: Thoughts on TFT's Design

content:
Link to Game # https://suareal.itch.io/websters
Team Size/Time constraint # Main programmer and designer in a team of 2. Made in 2 days for a game jam. What I did # Came up with the core concept and designed the full game loop Programmed the vast majority of the game, including: Online multiplayer with FishNet, keeping every player’s state, turns, and submissions in sync Round flow through the prompt, define, decoy, and guess phases Building each round’s word bank from players’ prompt answers plus 10 random dictionary words The definition builder, which restricts the definer to words from the bank Decoy submission, shuffling decoys in with the real word, and guess handling Game Overview # Websters is a Jackbox-style party game about defining a word with completely unrelated words, leading to nonsensical definitions, and a lot of questioning of your friends’ intelligence. Gameplay Loop # Prompt: Every player answers a prompt. Their answers become the shared word bank for the round. Define: One player picks a secret word and has to describe it using only words from the bank. Ten random dictionary words are thrown in too, to help fill in gaps. Decoy: Everyone else reads the description they wrote and writes a decoy/fake word they think fits it. Guess: All the decoys are revealed alongside the real word, and everyone tries to pick out the real one. For example, if my prompt answer was “I really enjoy eating pancakes” and my secret word is cannibal, I have to describe a cannibal with “I, really, enjoy, eating, pancakes,” plus whatever everyone else wrote and the random words.
summary: A Jackbox-style party game where you define a word using only everyone elses words
title: Websters

Link to Game # https://charliedreemur.itch.io/holoswipe
Team Size/Time constraint # Worked as a programmer and designer in a team of 4, for a 2 week long Game Jam. What I did # Wrote initial game concept summary Programmed disasters, loot drops, player stats, UI, and Sound Designed and balanced player stats, items, and disasters Game Overview # Holoswipe is a fast-paced 3d roguelike where the objective is to survive one week as an obsessed Hololive Fan. Each day you must buy run around booths to collect coins and buy enough merch to prove your allegiance. Merch items give you stats in return which can increase your income, discount items, or help you avoid money-stealing disasters. Gameplay Design # The goal of the game is to get enough fan score each day to reach the next day. This is similar to games like balatro, where the only objective is to get your score high enough to win.
Money: Players obtain money in 2 ways, through coins which spawn randomly and frequently around the map and salary, a flat sum of money which is
Items: Items will spawn in set areas in the map, and can be bought with money. With some exceptions, item spawns will always be random, though the location they spawn is the same each time. Items are the core of the gameplay, and the only way for players to increase their stats and fanscore enough to reach the target. The goal of random item spawns is to offer a different experience/item build for multiple playthroughs.
Limited inventory: Players have a limited space to hold items, and players can organize their inventory to hold more. This allows for a slight optimization minigame, as well as providing for more item balancing levers (items that are cheaper are stronger earlier on when inventory space isn’t an issue, whereas items that take up less space are more useful later when the player has a strong economy built). Additionally, it’s simply cool to see the item sprites in your inventory.
Disasters: Disasters are thematic events which can impede the player’s movement, or steal their money. These are mainly intended to keep players on their toes and moving all the time, increasing tension, as well as providing homage to Hololive members.
Loot spawns: Loot spawns are the counterpart to disasters. Since the player can simply leave the convention early if they want, these loot spawns incentivize the player to stay in the convention for as long as they can, as well as providing exciting moments where players can be dropped expensive items.
Time limit: Each day, there is a time limit before the player will be chased out by enemies which get increasingly faster and deduct a large sum of money if they reach. The idea behind these enemies is to allow a slight bit of leeway to the player, as well as letting players to feel how much “stronger” they are later in the game. Since the enemies slowly scale up their speed, high speed builds will be able to run from them for longer, and create fun moments.
Item Balance # Overall philosophy: While testing, I found that there were numerous times where the best strategy was simply amassing a large sum of fan score through items (As opposed to other items which offer other stats in addition such as luck, movespeed, or discount). While optimal, it felt terrible, as the items the player would buy would keep them at near base stats throughout the entire playthrough, resulting in them feeling the same at the end of the game as they do at the start. Because of this, a lot of the stat allocation and balancing is intended to incentivize players to get a wide variety of stats so they feel much stronger by the end, almost as though they’re cheating compared to the start. Most viable builds will include comically high speed, enough luck to make it rain loot, or so much discount that items are practically free, allowing for a satisfying sense of progression.
Posters and pins: special items which give increased stats based on the other items in your inventory. These are the cruxes of our archetypes, and powerful items which players should feel happy to build around.
Plushies: Items which always spawn in the same location and give pure fanscore. These are intentionally extremely understatted for 2 reasons: The fact that these always spawn means that they would reduce variation and replayability. Additionally, since they don’t give any stat other than fanscore, they don’t make the player feel any stronger. However, they are useful later on, as they take up very little space, and players who have an excess of money can buy them to fill in their empty inventory slots efficiently.
summary: A fast paced shopping spree roguelike created for HoloJam 6

Your browser does not support the video tag. Team Size/Time constraint # Worked as the lead of design in a team of 9, starting in Oct 2024, currently ongoing. What I did # Lead all design decisions, working in several design disciplines such as Mechanics, Technical, UX, QA etc. Authored 20+ design documents, including Gameplay Loops, Feature Breakdowns, Asset Lists, etc. Worked in Unreal Engine using Blueprint and C++ to implement and balance level designs Game Overview # In Master Dancer, you meet the famous dancer Loïe Fuller, the first to integrate technology into modern dance. As a player, you engage in action games to learn her movement principles and, guided by Virtual Loïe, explore her world. You will use modern VR technology to create your own unique dance, becoming a Master Dancer yourself! Star Maker # Star maker is one of the minigames meant to teach players dance principles. In this game, players must hit orbs flying at them towards targets in time with the music. The core design pillars of Star Maker are to teach players to do strong, direct movements, have players feel in tune with the music, and to be very forgiving in gameplay.
Notable Features # Designed an orb trajectory prediction system so that the orb hits targets when it appears to from the player’s perspective. Designed an aim assist feature to make game feel more satisfying. The strength is linearly curved so that wildly inaccurate hit will still be very off, while closer hits will hit the target. Adjusted aim assist strength through multiple playtest sessions. Designed a music looping system in order to give players multiple tries, reducing frustrayion while maintaining the musicality of the game. Music Roundabout # Music Roundabout (called Music Game while in development) is another minigame meant to teach players dance principles. In this game, players will activate orbs which rotate around them, creating a melody. The core design pillars of Music Roundabout are to teach players twisting motion, as well as a light tapping motion. In addition, players should feel as though they are creating music as they play.
Notable Features # Designed an orb charging system where players had to follow the rotating orb with their hand to incentivize players to twist their hips naturally. Designed visual indicators for players to know when to activate orbs, even with no sound (Although, sound was of course vital for this minigame). Chose to limit the arc of the orb, from traversing in a full circle to a half circle, to prevent players from getting dizzy and tangled in the VR headset’s wire. Examples of Work # Mockup/Art Reference for some of the tutorial systems. Art reference board for the “Hub Room” of the game.
